lesson.subtitle: Lesson 15 -- Turning Point (Block Checkpoint)
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Henrique Tadeu Alves da Silva | Lesson 15 -- Turning Point (Block Checkpoint)

listenings.text: When I look back on my career, the real turning point was not a big success. It was a small disaster. I was twenty-four, and I was working as a backing singer on a TV show. One night, the lead singer lost her voice an hour before the live broadcast, and the producer asked me to sing her part. I said yes before I really made up my mind. It was by far the most frightening night of my life. I forgot a few words in the second verse, and the next day the show was criticized in two newspapers. That was a setback, of course. But a week later, a songwriter called me. She told me that my voice sounded honest, and she asked me to sing on her demo. That demo was my stepping stone. I used to think that a mistake was the end of the story. Now I tell my students that the important part is not how you fall. It is how you bounce back.

For six years, I edited sound for commercials. The money was good, and I was very comfortable. Too comfortable. Then a director I worked with said something that I still remember. He told me that my work was clean, but that it had no personality. That was my wake-up call. I made up my mind to study film sound, and I applied to a course in London. The course was taught by people who worked on real films, and I was the oldest student in the class. In the first month, I was much slower than the younger students, and I hardly understood their jokes. But I had a lot of experience, and very few of them did. Slowly, it paid off. Today I work on documentaries, and my work is nowhere near as clean as it used to be. It is a lot more interesting. If you have been comfortable for too long, that is a sign. It is probably time to get out of your comfort zone.

extra_audio.text: In 2018, I was working in TV in Brazil. I made up my mind to study color grading in Seoul for six months. I didn't speak Korean, so every class was taught in English. In the first week, I hardly said anything. My teacher told me that I understood much more than I said. Looking back, that trip was the turning point for my English.
